query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A post-sintering heat treatment of mechanically alloyed Mg–Ti–Zn high‐entropy alloys drives a controlled transformation of metastable phases, which in turn promotes the surface enrichment of reactive Ti and Zn that form protective oxide layers. This microstructural evolution enhances both corrosion resistance and high‐temperature oxidation behavior relative to the as-sintered (non-heat-treated) state.
generation.material_initial_state: Mechanically alloyed, as-sintered lightweight Mg–Ti–Zn high-entropy alloy (density < 6 g/cm³) exhibiting a mixture of solid solution and metastable intermetallic phases.
generation.intervention: Post-sintering heat treatment at an elevated temperature (under controlled time-temperature conditions) designed to trigger phase transformations and promote reactive element diffusion toward surfaces.
generation.conditions: A controlled laboratory setting comparing two sets of samples: one receiving the post-sintering heat treatment and one maintained in the as-sintered state, with all other processing parameters held constant.
generation.structural_mediator: The heat treatment-induced formation and redistribution of stable intermetallic phases and the corresponding segregation of Ti and Zn at grain boundaries and near-surface regions, leading to in situ formation of TiO₂- and/or ZnO-rich passivating oxide layers.
generation.mechanism: Elevated heat treatment accelerates diffusional kinetics, causing the metastable microstructure to evolve into a more thermodynamically stable configuration. This evolution promotes the selective oxidation of Ti and Zn at the alloy surfaces and along internal boundaries, thereby establishing a protective oxide scale that retards both corrosive attack in ambient aqueous environments and degradation under high-temperature oxidation conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-sintered baseline, the heat-treated alloy will exhibit lower corrosion current densities (indicative of enhanced corrosion resistance) and reduced oxide scale thickness and mass loss during high-temperature oxidation tests.
generation.baseline: The initial as-sintered state of the mechanically alloyed Mg–Ti–Zn high-entropy alloy, which is expected to show a less defined oxide passivation and higher susceptibility to corrosion and high-temperature oxidation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy systems processed via mechanical alloying and sintering, with alloy compositions featuring Mg, Ti, and Zn, and a density constraint below 6 g/cm³. It may not hold for alloys with significantly different compositions or for those processed by routes other than mechanical alloying followed by sintering.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvements in corrosion and oxidation resistance remains uncertain and is likely sensitive to the specific heat treatment parameters (temperature, duration, atmosphere) and the precise alloy composition. Additional work is needed to optimize these parameters for maximal benefit.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mg–Ti–Zn high-entropy alloy samples using identical mechanical alloying and sintering processes. Subject one set to a defined post-sintering heat treatment while keeping the other set as-sintered. Expose both sets to standardized corrosion tests (e.g., NaCl aqueous solution) and high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., at 850°C in air) for specified durations.
measurements: Electrochemical corrosion metrics (corrosion current density, impedance spectroscopy)
Mass loss measurements and oxide scale thickness (via cross-sectional SEM/EDS analysis) after high-temperature oxidation
Microstructural characterization before and after testing (using XRD, SEM, and EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in corrosion resistance (e.g., similar or higher corrosion current densities) and high-temperature oxidation performance (e.g., similar or greater oxide scale thickness and mass loss) compared to the as-sintered samples, then the hypothesis that the post-sintering heat treatment improves functional performance via the proposed phase evolution mechanism will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One promising design strategy involves the development of multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), which incorporate multiple elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios to achieve property combinations beyond those achievable in conventional binary or ternary systems. While this concept has been widely explored in high-entropy alloys, its application to Mg-rich systems remains limited and may offer new pathways for improving corrosion resistance, mechanical performance, and maintaining a low density. While prior studies have investigated Mg-Ti, Mg-Zn, and Zn-Ti binary alloys individually, the combined effects of Ti and Zn in bulk Mg-rich multi-element systems remain poorly understood, particularly with respect to phase stability, passivation behavior, and mechanical properties.

Several studies have explored Mg-Zn, Mg-Ti, and Zn-Ti alloys for their potential to improve corrosion resistance and mechanical performance [,,,,]. Mg-Zn alloys have been shown to promote grain refinement and ZnO-rich surface films, with corrosion current densities (icorr) typically ranging from 10 to 100 µA/cm2 in NaCl solutions, although their poor hardness (less than ~1 GPa) limits their broader implementation []. Ti additions to Mg offer excellent corrosion resistance, often reducing icorr to the range of 1–10 µA/cm2, but are hindered by poor solubility in Mg and higher cost [,]. However, sputtered Mg-Ti films have demonstrated passivation via TiO2-rich layers and reduced current densities, although this line of study lacks bulk validation []. Binary Zn-Ti alloys have shown promising corrosion resistance (e.g., ~2 µA/cm2) and improved surface passivation due to Ti rich phases, but still face challenges in balancing degradation rate with mechanical robustness []. Recent work by Mukhtar et al. demonstrated that mechanical alloying followed by compaction and sintering can successfully produce bulk Mg-Ti-Zn alloys with refined nanostructures and enhanced mechanical properties []. Lightweight complex concentrated alloys (LWCCA), composed of elements with low density, have become a great area of interest due to the high demand in a large number of applications. Previous research on LWCCAs was focused on high entropy multicomponent alloy systems that provide low density and high capability of solid solution formation. Present research introduces two alloy systems (Al-Cu-Si-Zn-Mg and Al-Mn-Zn-Mg-Si) that contain readily available and inexpensive starting materials and have potential for solid solution formation structures. For the selection of appropriate compositions, authors applied semi-empirical criteria and optimization software. Specialized modeling software (MatCalc) was used to determine probable alloy structures by CALPHAD, non-equilibrium solidification and kinetic simulations. The selected alloys were prepared in an induction furnace. Specimens were heat treated to provide stable structures. Physicochemical, microstructural, and mechanical characterization was performed for the selected alloy compositions. reading.lever: Post-sintering heat treatment of mechanically alloyed Mg–Ti–Zn alloys to trigger metastable phase evolution and promote protective oxide formation.
reading.why: This combined processing route, evidenced in related Mg–Ti and Mg–Zn systems, directly addresses the need to elucidate transformation kinetics affecting corrosion and high-temperature oxidation in non-equilibrium lightweight HEAs.
